text:
Keep the Joins: Why Primary Schools Should Still Teach Joined-Up Handwriting

Every few years, someone declares that handwriting is finished. Keyboards are everywhere, the argument goes, so children should spend their precious classroom hours on coding or critical thinking instead of looping their letters together. Some education systems have already acted on this. Finland stopped requiring cursive in 2016, and several American states dropped it from their standards after the Common Core reforms, though a number have since reversed course. The case against joined-up writing sounds modern and practical. I think it is mistaken. Primary schools should keep teaching it, and teach it well, because it serves children's reading, spelling, thinking and confidence in ways that no keyboard can replace.

Start with what the critics get right. Adults rarely write long passages by hand. Most of what a child produces in secondary school and beyond will be typed. Joined-up writing is not a moral good in itself, and plenty of people with messy or print-style handwriting lead successful lives. If the choice were between teaching a decorative skill and teaching something essential, the decorative skill should lose. But that framing misdescribes what joined writing is. It is not decoration. It is a motor skill with cognitive payoffs, and the cost of teaching it is small compared with what it returns.

The first payoff is fluency. Printing requires the writer to lift the pen after every letter, which breaks the movement of each word into separate stabs. A joined script lets the hand travel through a whole word in one flowing motion. Once a child has mastered it, the speed gain is real. Research from several countries, including studies of children moving from print to cursive in the middle primary years, suggests that fluent joined writers can produce text faster without a loss of legibility. For a child who needs to get ideas onto paper before they evaporate, speed matters. A slow, laboured hand is a bottleneck between a mind full of things to say and a page that stays stubbornly empty. Reducing that bottleneck is among the kindest things a school can do for a struggling writer.

The second payoff concerns spelling and the structure of words. When a child joins letters, the word becomes a single physical unit with a rhythm. The hand learns that the letters in a word belong together, that certain sequences travel as a group. Think of the way a child who writes the ending of a word in one smooth stroke gradually stops misplacing letters within it. Teachers who work with children with dyslexia have long reported that cursive can help, because the continuous movement reduces reversals of letters such as b and d and discourages the habit of starting letters in the wrong place. The evidence here is not airtight, and it would be dishonest to claim it is. But the practical experience of specialist teachers is consistent enough that dropping the approach on the strength of a fashionable assumption would be reckless.

The third payoff is the one that deserves the most attention, because it is the best supported. Handwriting is not just a way of recording language. It is a way of processing it. Brain imaging work by researchers such as Karin James at Indiana University has shown that children who practise forming letters by hand activate reading-related regions of the brain more strongly than children who only type or trace them. Studies of adults and students have found that taking notes by hand leads to better conceptual understanding than typing them, partly because the slowness of the hand forces the writer to select, compress and rephrase rather than transcribe. A child who learns to write fluently by hand is building a thinking tool that stays with them. Joined writing, with its demand for continuous coordination, is the most developed form of that tool.

Some will object that this is an argument for handwriting in general, not for joined handwriting in particular. Fair enough. A child who prints neatly gets many of these benefits. But the objection does not survive contact with how schools actually work. Teaching two scripts, print and then cursive, is a standard sequence for good reason. Print is easy to learn and matches the letters in books. Joining is a refinement that builds on it, and it can be introduced gradually, often from around seven, once the basic letter shapes are secure. The alternative, which is to stay in print forever, leaves children with a style that is slower for most of them at speed and that tends to degrade into an unreadable scrawl when they are pressed for time. A taught joined hand gives a child something to fall back on, a model of efficient movement, rather than leaving each one to invent a personal system by accident.

There is also an argument from equality, and it is easy to overlook. Children from homes full of books, devices and patient adults will find ways to practise whatever they need. Children from homes with fewer of these resources depend on school to teach the physical craft of writing. If handwriting instruction is dropped from the timetable, the children who suffer first are those who cannot make it up elsewhere. The same is true of access to keyboards. Not every child has a laptop at home, and a school that assumes typing will do the work of handwriting is assuming a level of household provision that cannot be taken for granted. Handwriting costs a pencil and a sheet of paper. It is among the cheapest and most democratic skills a school can pass on.

A related point concerns reading. A child who never learns joined script will not be able to read it. That sounds trivial until you consider how much of the world's written record is handwritten. Letters from grandparents, annotations in family recipe books, historical documents, the comments a teacher writes in a margin, even the birthday card from a great-aunt, all arrive in a joined hand. A generation that cannot read cursive is cut off from a layer of its own culture, and has to rely on transcription by others. Primary schools teach children to read a great many things that are not strictly necessary for passing exams, from the clock face to the map. Joined writing belongs in that company.

Then there is the matter of identity and pleasure. A signature is a joined-up gesture. It is one of the first things a child learns that feels adult, a mark that says this is mine. Many children take real pride in developing a handwriting that looks like them. This is not frivolous. Confidence is a large part of what makes a young writer persist, and the visible, tangible improvement that comes from practising a skill with the hand gives children a clear sense that effort pays off. A page of well-formed writing is something a child can look at and be proud of in a way that a screen of identical typed characters rarely provides.

What about the claim that the time could be better spent? Here the numbers matter. Good handwriting instruction does not need long sessions. Ten to fifteen minutes a day, woven into the routine of writing lessons, is enough for most children to become competent over a couple of years. That is a tiny fraction of a school week. Meanwhile the time freed by abolishing it would not obviously go to anything better. If the proposal is to replace joined writing with typing lessons, note that children pick up typing readily, usually outside school and at a later age, and that keyboard skill develops well on top of a secure foundation in handwriting, not instead of one. If the proposal is to replace it with coding, one should ask what a six-year-old gains from learning to write loops in a programming language before learning to write loops on a page.

None of this requires nostalgia or rigid drilling. The old picture of a stern teacher rapping knuckles over a smudged copybook is a bad model. Good handwriting teaching is short, warm and varied. It uses large movements before small ones, pairs practice with real writing about things children care about, and accepts that a child's final style will be their own. It adapts for left-handed writers, for children with motor difficulties, and for those who will always find it hard. Where a child genuinely cannot manage it, a keyboard is the right tool, and no one should be penalised for needing it. The aim is to give every child who can learn it a fluent, legible, comfortable hand, and to treat the exceptions with flexibility.

Schools should also resist the temptation to treat this as a binary contest between pen and keyboard. Children will need both, and the sensible position is that each should be taught properly. The danger in the current debate is that handwriting is dismissed as a relic by people who learned it so thoroughly that they no longer notice the cognitive work it once did for them. The skill feels automatic to an adult precisely because someone invested the time to make it so. Removing that investment from the next generation does not free them from the need for the skill. It only makes them acquire it badly, or not at all.

So the answer is yes. Primary schools should continue to teach joined-up handwriting. It speeds up writing, supports spelling, strengthens the link between hand and mind, keeps children connected to the handwritten world around them, serves those with the fewest resources, and gives young writers a tangible source of pride. The cost is a few minutes a day. The benefits last a lifetime. Dropping the joins would be a quiet loss, dressed up as progress, and one that we would struggle to reverse once a generation had grown up without it.
